strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: forecasting pretraining loss early enough to guide decisions on the target model. The decomposition into token-position losses provides an interpretable empirical approach.

The experiments extend beyond fitting observed trajectories: forecasts on 468M, 1.2B, and 6.7B models outperform the reported baselines on both ID and OOD validation data. Additional GPT-NeoX and MoE fits broaden the descriptive evidence.

The data-mixture application includes completed 400B-token training runs and seven downstream benchmarks. The selected mixtures achieve lower reported perplexity at both target model sizes, providing useful evidence of potential practical value.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not establish the benefit of token-position decomposition. Once Eq. (8) freezes a0 and a1, Eq. (10) reduces to a constant plus a2(N). A direct aggregate-loss predictor using the same piecewise log-log/cosine structure and known learning-rate schedule is therefore an essential control. The current power-law, reciprocal, and logarithmic baselines cannot distinguish benefits of decomposition from benefits of incorporating the schedule. All experiments use cosine decay, further limiting the generic-law claim.

Important reproduction details remain unspecified despite the useful configuration tables and pseudocode: the outlier-rejection rule, nonlinear-fitting initialization and constraints, evaluation interval, and actual data-mixture candidates. Algorithm 1, lines 29–30, also applies calibration before the separation point, whereas Section 2.4 specifies calibration using observations after it. These ambiguities directly affect the forecasting procedure.

Evidence for reliable hyperparameter selection is limited. Table 4's perplexity improvements are only 0.05–0.15, without uncertainty estimates or independent training repetitions; averaging the last five checkpoints does not establish robustness. Candidate-level predicted versus final losses and ranking accuracy are absent. Moreover, selection uses 10B tokens, or 2.5% of training, while the forecasting evaluation starts at 10%, leaving accuracy at the practical selection budget insufficiently characterized.

The theoretical interpretations exceed their justification. Appendix C rejects exponential decay after setting its additive offset to zero, although an exponential with a positive offset can satisfy the stated nonzero-loss asymptote. Equation (17) follows from manually freezing two fitted parameters and does not establish that positional reweighting is unnecessary. Figure 11 and the three suppression experiments provide narrower empirical support, with several near ties in Table 10.

The novelty framing inadequately distinguishes this work from existing learning-curve modeling. Kaplan et al. (2020) already analyze loss as a function of optimization steps, so describing prior scaling laws as exclusively modeling final losses is misleading. The contribution should be positioned around the particular positional decomposition and forecasting procedure.

Some accuracy statements contradict the presented results. Section 2.3 claims R² > 0.99 across settings, but Table 2 includes 0.9858 and 0.9795. Section 2.4 claims MSE < 0.01 throughout, but Figure 3 shows larger early-prefix errors for the 6.7B model. These discrepancies do not negate the relative improvements, but require correction. The positive empirical evidence makes Findings plausible; the unresolved comparison and reproducibility concerns prevent a clear acceptance recommendation.
